passage.title: Eighty-Five Voices on Paper
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
In the early 1800s, a Cherokee silversmith named Sequoyah watched white soldiers and traders read letters on folded sheets of paper. They called these sheets talking leaves. The ink marks on the page carried words across hundreds of miles. At that time, the Cherokee tongue was spoken across Georgia and nearby states. Still, it had no written form. Sequoyah believed his people could put their own speech on paper. Then they could preserve their laws and news without asking strangers for help.

At first, Sequoyah tried to make a separate small drawing for each word in his tongue. After months of carving marks onto thin strips of birch bark, he realized that thousands of individual word pictures would be impossible for anyone to memorize. Still, he did not quit. He listened closely to how friends spoke around the camp fire. Soon he spotted a clear rule. Every long word was built from a small set of distinct spoken sounds.

Working patiently for twelve years, Sequoyah sorted every sound in his language until he had a complete chart of eighty-five symbols. Each mark stood for one short sound, such as 'ga' or 'no.' Because the chart matched the exact sounds that Cherokee speakers already used every day, learners did not have to spend years studying silent letters or confusing spelling rules. In 1821, Sequoyah and his young girl walked in to show the new chart to the town chiefs. Skeptical council elders, convinced at first that written marks were a trick of memory, were soon amazed by the rapid messages shared between father and daughter.

Once the chiefs backed the chart, a wave of learning swept through the towns. A speaker needed to learn only eighty-five sound marks. Both kids and old folks mastered reading in just a few weeks. Families painted the symbols on cabin walls and taught neighbors along rural trails. Within five years, most people in the tribe could read and write in their own tongue.

By 1828, leaders in New Echota, Georgia, had metal type cast in those marks. They started a weekly paper called the Cherokee Phoenix. Printed side by side in Cherokee and English, the paper carried tribal laws, local news, and stories to readers across the nation. Without ever going to school himself, Sequoyah had given his people a lasting voice in print.

tier2Words.definition: to keep something safe from being lost or forgotten over time
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root servare ('to keep safe or guard') + prefix pre- ('before')
tier2Words.contextClue: Sequoyah wanted his people to capture their speech on paper so they could save their laws and news for the future.

tier2Words.definition: clearly separate and different from others
tier2Words.rootHint: Latin root distinguere ('to separate or mark off')

tier2Words.definition: having doubts and not easily convinced that something is true
tier2Words.rootHint: From Greek skeptikos, meaning 'thoughtful or questioning'
tier2Words.contextClue: The council elders doubted the system at first and thought the written marks were just a trick of memory.

tier2Words.definition: learned a skill completely and became very good at it

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 3:

"Skeptical council elders, convinced at first that written marks were a trick of memory, were soon amazed by the rapid messages shared between father and daughter."

Based on the structure of the sentence, who felt amazed, and what caused their amazement?

options.text: White soldiers in New Echota were amazed by the metal printing press inside the cabin.
options.childFeedback: White soldiers were mentioned back in Paragraph 1, and the metal printing press in New Echota was not made until 1828 in Paragraph 5.

options.text: Sequoyah and his daughter felt amazed because the council elders played a memory trick on them.
options.childFeedback: This flips the people around! Sequoyah and his daughter were the ones sharing written messages, and the skeptical council elders were the ones who felt amazed.

options.text: A trick of memory amazed the written marks and stopped the father from speaking to the council.
options.childFeedback: Written marks cannot feel amazed! At first the elders thought the marks were a memory trick, until the rapid messages amazed them.

options.text: The council elders felt amazed, and the rapid messages shared between Sequoyah and his daughter caused their amazement.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'Skeptical council elders... were soon amazed by the rapid messages shared between father and daughter' shows that the council elders felt amazed, and the rapid messages between Sequoyah and his daughter caused their amazement.

questions.provingSentenceText: Skeptical council elders, convinced at first that written marks were a trick of memory, were soon amazed by the rapid messages shared between father and daughter.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 3, 'Skeptical council elders... were soon amazed by the rapid messages shared between father and daughter' shows that the council elders felt amazed, and the rapid messages between Sequoyah and his daughter caused their amazement.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive sentence, 'Skeptical council elders' is the receiver of the verb 'were soon amazed', and 'the rapid messages shared between father and daughter' is the agent after 'by'.
questions.retryHint: Look at the subject ('Skeptical council elders') and the 'by' phrase after 'were soon amazed' in Paragraph 3.

What does the word skeptical mean as it is used in Paragraph 3?

options.text: Skilled at working with silver and metal printing type

options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 3, 'skeptical' means doubtful and unsure whether something is truly real, because the council elders thought at first that the written marks were just a trick of memory.

options.text: Tired from walking hundreds of miles along forest trails
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 mentions letters carrying words across hundreds of miles, not that the council elders were tired from walking forest trails.

questions.prompt: Based on Paragraph 2, why did Sequoyah abandon his first plan for writing down the Cherokee language?

options.text: He ran out of birch bark in the woods and could not buy paper from the traders.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 never says he ran out of birch bark; he stopped making word pictures because thousands of separate drawings were too many to memorize.

options.text: He realized that making a separate picture for every word would create too many symbols to remember.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 2 explains that after months of carving separate drawings for each word onto birch bark, Sequoyah realized that thousands of individual word pictures would be impossible for anyone to memorize.

options.text: The tribal council passed a law forbidding anyone from carving marks onto trees.
options.childFeedback: The tribal council never banned carving marks on bark; in fact, the chiefs backed Sequoyah's finished chart in Paragraph 4.

options.text: He decided that English spelling rules were much easier to learn than Cherokee sounds.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 points out that Sequoyah's Cherokee sound chart avoided silent letters and confusing spelling rules.

questions.provingSentenceText: After months of carving marks onto thin strips of birch bark, he realized that thousands of individual word pictures would be impossible for anyone to memorize.

questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 2 explains that Sequoyah gave up on word pictures because 'thousands of individual word pictures would be impossible for anyone to memorize.'
questions.retryHint: Read the second sentence of Paragraph 2 to see what Sequoyah realized after months of carving marks on birch bark.

questions.prompt: Which reason does the author give in Paragraphs 3 and 4 to explain why Cherokee speakers could learn to read Sequoyah's syllabary in just a few weeks?

options.text: Each of the eighty-five symbols matched a single spoken syllable that Cherokee speakers already used every day.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 3 and 4 explain that because the eighty-five symbols matched the exact spoken sounds Cherokee speakers already used every day, people did not have to study silent letters or tricky spelling rules and could learn in weeks.

options.text: Every Cherokee town built large brick schoolhouses staffed by teachers from New Echota.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says families painted the symbols on cabin walls and taught neighbors along rural trails, rather than building large brick schoolhouses.

options.text: The syllabary used only five symbols so learners never had to write long sentences.
options.childFeedback: The chart had eighty-five symbols—not just five—and people learned all eighty-five within a few weeks because they matched spoken syllables.

options.text: Readers only needed to look at the English column of the Cherokee Phoenix to understand the marks.
options.childFeedback: Most Cherokee speakers learned the eighty-five symbols years before the bilingual Cherokee Phoenix newspaper started in 1828.

questions.provingSentenceText: Because the chart matched the exact sounds that Cherokee speakers already used every day, learners did not have to spend years studying silent letters or confusing spelling rules.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 3 and 4 explain that because the eighty-five symbols matched the exact spoken sounds Cherokee speakers already used every day, people did not have to study silent letters or tricky spelling rules and could learn in weeks.
questions.parentExplanation: To support the claim that the syllabary was easy to master (ELAGSE5RI8), the author explains that each of the 85 symbols stood for one exact spoken syllable without silent letters or irregular spelling rules.
questions.retryHint: Read the third sentence of Paragraph 3 to see why learners did not have to spend years studying silent letters or spelling rules.

questions.prompt: Part A: Which claim made by the author in Paragraph 1 is best supported by the evidence in Paragraph 5?

options.text: Working as a silversmith was the best way to earn money in early nineteenth-century Georgia.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 1 only mentions that Sequoyah was a silversmith to introduce him; the passage never discusses ways to earn money.

options.text: Capturing Cherokee speech on paper would allow the nation to preserve and share its own laws and news.
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 1, Sequoyah believed that putting Cherokee speech on paper would let his people preserve their laws and news, and Paragraph 5 proves this came true when the Cherokee Phoenix printed tribal laws, local news, and stories.

options.text: Birch bark strips were stronger and lasted longer than printed newspaper pages.
options.childFeedback: Birch bark is only mentioned in Paragraph 2 when Sequoyah tested his first drawings; it is never compared to newspaper strength in Paragraph 5.

options.text: No one can invent a useful writing system without attending college first.
options.childFeedback: The final sentence of Paragraph 5 proves the exact opposite: 'Without ever going to school himself, Sequoyah had given his people a lasting voice in print.'

questions.provingSentenceText: Printed side by side in Cherokee and English, the paper carried tribal laws, local news, and stories to readers across the nation.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 1, Sequoyah believed that putting Cherokee speech on paper would let his people preserve their laws and news, and Paragraph 5 proves this came true when the Cherokee Phoenix printed tribal laws, local news, and stories.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 1, Sequoyah believed a writing system would let his people 'preserve their laws and news'; Paragraph 5 proves this came true when the Cherokee Phoenix printed tribal laws and local news across the nation.
questions.retryHint: Compare Sequoyah's goal at the end of Paragraph 1 ('preserve their laws and news') with what the Cherokee Phoenix newspaper printed in Paragraph 5.
